links.reason: The contrast is real and pointed: in 28 he sees the boy (கண்டு) but does not say stop (நில்லென்னாது) and drives on (நோக்கான் தேர் ஊர்ந்து), in Akananuru 66 he cries நெடுந்தேர் தாங்குமதி வலவ and climbs down. Puram 34's செய்தி கொன்றோர்க்கு உய்தி இல் and Kali 149's ஒற்கத்துள் உதவியார்க்கு உதவாதான் ... எறியாது விடாதே do share the rule against ingratitude. The question is the same, almost in the same words: காதலன் பின்போதல் வல்லவோ மாதர் நடை (37) and காளைபின் நாளை நடக்கவும் வல்லையோ (Naladiyar 398). The first doubts the feet by her stumbling at play by the ford (வீழ்பவள் போலத் தளருங்கால்), and the second answers with the horse proverb that the skill comes with the thing. That is a real clash of claims about her ability. The mother as speaker of 37 is inferred, since the colophon gives no thurai, but this is the standard paalai voice.

The formula is real: கலிங்கத்துள் ஒடுங்கிய (Kali 69) and கோடிக் கலிங்கத்து ஒடுங்கினள் (Ak 86). But in Ak 86 the curled bride is on the first night, after the rite, not at it. The claim of 'two wedding rites' rests on silence: Ak 86 does not mention fire, and that does not show the rite had none. Same image is the honest type, and the ritual conclusion is overstated.

Natrinai 269 sets the son climbing down his chest (மார்பு ஊர்பு இழிய) and the wife's roving eyes (கண் இணைந்து அலமரும்) before a man who would cross the hills, and Kural 1151 threatens her death. The difference in tactic is real. But the pairing rests on the colophon's alternative thurai (செலவு அழுங்குவித்ததூஉம் ஆம்) and on Parimelazhagar's choice of speaker for the couplet. The couplet itself names no friend, so 'one option among the friend's arguments' is built on commentary.

Both are the mighty man undone by something small: the hatchling (குருளை) and the elephant (கான யானை அணங்கியாங்கு) on one side, ஒண்ணுதற்கோ உடைந்ததே on the other. But அணங்கு is to afflict as a spirit does, and 'poison not strength' is not in the Tamil. The claim that the poem 'explains why the couplet's warrior has no defence' credits the Kuruntokai with a link it does not make. What the two share is the topic of the small undoing the great.

The same poet (ஒளவையார்) names the same patron: நெடு மான் அஞ்சி ... தேர் வீசு இருக்கை போல மாரி இரீஇ (Nat 381) and Athiyaman of the elephants and chariots, whose gift is as sure as கோட்டிடை வைத்த கவளம் (Puram 101). The note says exactly what the akam poem does with the puram name: unfailing giving becomes the steady rain the waiting woman cannot bear. The pairing teaches something neither verse shows alone.

Ainkurunuru 127 only describes the rival (தும்பை மாலை இளமுலை நுண்பூண் ஆகம் விலங்குவோளே); nothing in it calls her laughable or 'of no account', and the marker itself flags the sense as uncertain. Natrinai 170 fears the rival's வன்மை, but it does not ground that in her youth. The 'incompatible claims about youth' are supplied by the proposer, not found in either poem.

Both neythal poems colour the shore through Balarama and Mal: மாயவனும் தம்முனும் போலே மறிகடலும் ... வெண்மணலும் (58) and பால் அன்ன மேனியான் ... நீல நீர் உடை போல ... வெண் திரை வால் எக்கர் (Kali 124). The teaches is accurate and specific. The Kali puts dark and white on the one white brother and his blue cloth, while the venba divides them between the two brothers.

Puram 216 makes the very claim of the couplet: கேட்டல் மாத்திரை அல்லது ... காண்டல் இல்லாது, friends by hearing alone. It uses the same technical word (கிழமையர், காதற் கிழமை against நட்பாங் கிழமை தரும்). The king's order to keep the seat (ஒழிக்க அவற்கு இடமே) is a concrete staking of the rule that புணர்ச்சி பழகுதல் வேண்டா.

The verbal echo is exact in sense: நிலையாப் பொருட்பிணி (Kur 350) and அற்கா இயல்பிற்றுச் செல்வம் (Kural 333). The akam friend turns the premise against the journey, since he left for what does not stay (செல்லாதீம் எனச் சொல்லினமாயின் செல்வர் கொல்லோ). That the lasting thing is her company is implied rather than said, but it is the natural reading of the contrast.

Paripadal 19.10-13 likens the finely dressed riders (புரி மாண் புரவியர், போக்கு அமை தேரர்) to அறம் பெரிது ஆற்றி அதன் பயன் கொண்மார் சிறந்தோர் உலகம் படருநர். That does touch Kural 37's palanquin-rider as the visible fruit of aram. But the teaches turns this into a history, the Kural 'taking a shared image of heavenly reward and pressing it' into this world, and neither text shows that borrowing. The Paripadal's ride is a festival simile, not a doctrine.

The shift of credit to the serpent is real. But 'a fixed myth could be re-credited to whichever power a cult served ... once it had a temple' generalises from one hymn and assumes a shrine the lines do not show. The hymn also praises the serpent's part without taking the deed from the bull-rider.

The scenes are not 'the same bare tree and kite': Kur 285 has a lone bird on the ஞெமை top craving flesh (ஊன் நசைஇ ஒருபருந்து), while Ain 321 has the hen kite calling from the forked ஓமை (ஓமை அம்கவட்டு ஏறி). The woman of 285 does not say he has forgotten her; she asks where he is and whether the mating call means nothing to his eyes. The 'answer from the other end of the road' is a construct laid over a stock paalai scene.

The two agree that the heart gives way when he comes: பேணி அவன் சிறிது அளித்தக் கால் என் நாண் இல் நெஞ்சம் நெகிழ்தல் (Kali 122) and கலந்துணர்த்தும் காதலர்க் கண்டால் (Kural 1246). But they differ on the anger. The Kural calls it false (பொய்க்காய்வு), while Kali 122's woman insists her grievance is real (அறிவேன் மன்) and answers the friend's ஏது இன்றி. So the Kural does not 'answer that reproach', and the Kali does not supply the couplet's setting.

The formula is the same, by the same poet: பாறை நெடுஞ்சுனை ... விளைந்த தேறல் in both, drunk unknowingly (அறியாது உண்ட / நீர்செத்து அயின்ற). Akananuru 2 draws the moral itself (குறியா இன்பம் ... குறித்த இன்பம் நினக்கு எவன் அரிய), while in the idyll the drunk peacock only marks the plenty of the man's land. The point that the image's force depends on its place in the speech is shown by the pair.

The verbal parallel is real: புல்லுநர் இல்லார் நடுங்கச் சிறுமாலை கொல்லுநர் போல வரும் against யாரும் இல் நெஞ்சினேம் ... ஈரும் இருள்மாலை. But the insight claimed, that the cruelty lies in the hearer's state, is stated wholly by Aimpathu 6 (செல்சார்வு உடையார்க்கு இனியவாய்). The pair adds only that Ezhupathu leaves the happy half unsaid, which is the shared topic of the cruel evening.

The teaches misreads Akananuru 98. Her fear is that if the god relieves her (வெறிகமழ் நெடுவேள் நல்குவனேயெனின்), the man will think her sickness was something else (செல்லலும் பிறிது). That turns on the god's power to cure a seizure (முருகன் ஆர் அணங்கு), not on his power to give husbands. Paripadal 19.89-94's elephant-leftover rite for winning husbands is a different power, and Ak 98 also mocks the diviners as பொய்வல் பெண்டிர் and மையற் பெண்டிர்.

links.reason: The two are close in wording: படரும் பனை ஈன்ற மாவும் சுடர் இழை நல்கியாள் நல்கியவை (Kali 138) and தந்தாள் மடலொடு மாலை உழக்கும் துயர் (Kural 1135). The shared detail is exact: கால் வல் தேர் கையின் இயக்க, நடை பயிற்றா (Kali 81) and தேர் நடைபயிற்றும் ... புதல்வன் (Nat 250). In both, the toddler with his toy chariot is the husband's way back, and the wife repels him: யாரையோ என்று இகந்து நின்றதுவே in one, நீ செல் in the other. So the son as the standing occasion of the return is shown across two anthologies.

Both men are sleepless: இரவினானும் துயிலறியேனே (Ain 172) and படல் ஒல்லா ... என் கண் (Kural 1136). But Ain 172 has nothing of the madal or of shame, and its sea simile is only restlessness. 'Sleeplessness as the stage just before shame is given up' is drawn from the Kural alone, so what the pair shares is the lover's insomnia.

Both split the woman from her weeping eyes, which saw him: தாம் தம் கெழுதகைமையின் அழுதன ... கண்ட எம் கண்ணே (Kur 241) and கண்தாம் கலுழ்வது எவன்கொலோ ... தாம் காட்ட (Kural 1171). The Kural charges the eyes as the cause, and the Kuruntokai gives them a right of intimacy, so the contrast is real. கெழுதகைமை could be ironic ('presuming on their intimacy'), but the difference in treatment holds on either reading.

Both charge the husband with bathing in the new flood with women: புதுப்புனல் ஆடக் கண்டோர் ... பலரே (Ain 64) and புதுப்புனல் ... ஆடினை என்ப (Ak 266). Ak 266 then sets the public gossip aside (இனி அஃது அவலம் அன்றுமன் எமக்கே) for the oath sworn before Murugan (சேஎயொடு உற்ற சூளே). That shift from witnesses to perjury is in the Tamil.

In Ain 234 the friend cites it as the cause of pallor: துன்னிக் கனவிற் காணும் இவளே நனவிற் காணாள் நின் மார்பே, with பசத்தல் and the slipping bangles. A friend's speech to the lover makes it pressure on him.

The phrase is shared, புன்கண் மாலை (Kur 46) and புன்கண்ணை ... மருள்மாலை (Kural 1222), and both test the absent man through the evening. One asks whether there is no evening where he went (இன்றுகொல் ... அவர் சென்ற நாட்டே), the other whether the evening's mate is as hard as hers. The premise is the same and the conclusions clash. Naladiyar 11 condemns those who delight in fleeting youth (மன்னா இளமை மகிழ்ந்தாரே கோல் ஊன்றி) and praises renouncing in childhood. Thinaimalai 85's taunt (வளமை கொணரும் வகையினால் ... இளமை கொணர இசை) argues that youth cannot be brought back and must be spent in love, not in getting wealth. On the plain reading these are incompatible counsels about delighting in youth.

The formula is shared: கொள்ளை சாற்றி and கொடுநுக ... ஒழுகை in both. But the given Perumpanatruppadai lines do not say the road is 'made safe for travellers by day under the patron'. The wording echoes closely: நின் முகம் தான் பெறின் அல்லது ... மருந்து பிறிது யாதும் இல் (Kali 60) and பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிறமன் ... தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து (Kural 1102). In Kali 60 the friend relays it to the girl as a plea, ending that sending him away is not kind. 'After union' for the Kural comes from its chapter placement, but the contrast of use holds.

Kur 14 plainly wishes for the town's knowing (அறிகதில் அம்ம இவ்வூரே ... நல்லோள் கணவன் இவன்). The difference in use is shown by the Tamil.

The shared idea is the lover as the cure: நோய்க்கு மருந்தாகிய கொண்கன் தேரே (Ain 101) and நோய்தணி காதலர் வர (Ak 22). But Ain 101 mentions no rite or remedy of the mother, so it does not 'correct' her remedy. Ak 22's mockery of the velan (ஏதில் வேலற்கு உலந்தமை) has no counterpart there, so the move from secret mockery to open correction is the proposer's construction.

The connection is real, a puram death recalled in an akam simile: எவ்வி வீழ்ந்த செருவில் பாணர் கைதொழு மரபின் முன் பரித்து இடூஉப் பழிச்சிய வள்உயிர் வணர்மருப்பு (Ak 115), and Puram 233's cry பொய்யாகியரோ at the report of Evvi's wounds. But there is no shared image: Puram 233 has no harps. The teaches is about words and gesture, which fits develops, and மரபின் does support 'a known rite'.

The farmer image is shared and used both ways. Verse 37 urges people to make provision like farmers who plough and sow (விளைநிலம் உழுவார்போல் வித்துநீர் செய்துகொண்மின்). Verse 42 shows ploughing without seed (வித்தின்றிப் பைங்கூழ் விளைக்குறல்) as the man without austerity (தவம் இல்லான்). Together they make the seed the point, not the labour.
links.text_issue: valayapathi:42 line 3 பொருளடு possibly பொருளொடு with a lost vowel sign

links.reason: Naladiyar 363 condemns the wife who does not enter the kitchen at dawn (அட்டில் புகாதாள்) or serve what she cooked (அட்டதனை உண்டி உதவாதாள்). Kur 167 shows a wife who cooks herself (தான் துழந்து அட்ட) and glows when he eats (நுண்ணிதின் மகிழ்ந்தன்று). Both endorse the same duty, so there is no incompatible claim. The difference is one of framing, threat against joy, which qualifies rather than contradicts.

The same poet uses the same task: படுபுலால் காப்பாள் (32), where the girl guarding the drying fish holds the man with her eyes, and படும்புலால் புட்கடிவான் புக்க ... இடம் (44), where the friend names that grove as the girl's place. The pair shows the fish watch doing in neythal what the millet watch does in kurinji, which neither verse says alone.

Ak 321's foster mother asks whether the girl rests in a hamlet (அம்குடிச் சீறூர் துணையொடு துச்சில் இருக்கும் கொல்லோ). Ain 382 is told from such a hamlet at nightfall (எல்லிடை அசைந்த கல்லென் சீறூர்), where mothers of daughters feel great pain (மனைகெழு பெண்டிர்க்கு நோவுமார் பெரிதே). The pair carries the mother's grief out to strangers on the road, which is in the Tamil of 382.

poems.note: The widowed monkey that dies is also an iraicchi-like act, but the scene maps part by part (dead mate to the man lost on the night path, the widow's death to the girl's), so it is ullurai.

iraicchi.act: having got the jackfruit, the male monkey calls its mate to share it
iraicchi.sense: the man should seek and claim her now that the mother keeps her from the field, not sulk

poems.note: The shore things are openly said to grieve as she does (போலும், எவன் கொலோ), which is open comparison.
No native thing beyond the town epithet; text is hard to construe.

iraicchi.act: feeds in the backwater but always returns to roost in the flowering grove
iraicchi.sense: wherever the man goes he returns to her, so the bond she calls hard to untie holds

iraicchi.act: the jungle hen goes with her cock to the slope and scratches up dust that shines with gold
iraicchi.sense: the lovers' going together on the hill will bring them good, so their bond should be one of love

poems.note: The vengai flowering and the mother's sending her to the field are season and opportunity, not a device.

iraicchi.act: the great tusker breaks the omai to ease the hunger of its young she-elephant
iraicchi.sense: even the beast tends its mate in the waste, so the heart that plans to leave her is harder than the beast

iraicchi.act: the tusker sleeps beside its mate in the omai's thin shade even in the burning waste
iraicchi.sense: even the beast keeps by its mate in the waste, so his going from her is the crueller

iraicchi.act: the she-monkey frolics with her mate on the rock by the hunters' yard
iraicchi.sense: the man should keep with her as the monkey pair keep together, not leave her eyes to pale

poems.note: The crow scene sits inside the open comparison of the town (அன்ன இவள்).

iraicchi.act: the young monkey runs and leaps freely in the grove
iraicchi.sense: her heart likewise roams unchecked to the man's chest

poems.note: Close to a mood parallel; tagged because the monkey's act matches the heart's act (உரையா வழங்கும்).
